questions.q: What are economic activities? How do they differ from non-economic activities?
answer: Economic activities are those that involve producing, exchanging or consuming goods and services, usually in order to earn an income and meet human needs and wants.

answer.text: A farmer growing crops for sale, a tailor stitching clothes, a shopkeeper selling goods, or a teacher taking paid classes are all doing economic activities.
Activities done out of love, duty or leisure, without any aim of earning, are non-economic — for example helping a friend, praying, or playing a game.
The key difference is the purpose: economic activities aim to produce income or satisfy wants through the market, while non-economic activities do not.

questions.q: Describe the three sectors of economic activity with examples.
answer: Economic activities are grouped into three sectors according to what they do.

answer.text: It obtains products directly from nature — agriculture, animal husbandry, fishing, forestry and mining. It is the base on which the others rest.
It manufactures goods by turning raw materials into finished products — for example making cloth from cotton or steel from iron ore.
It provides services that support the other two — transport, banking, trade, teaching, health, tourism and information technology.

answer: As an economy develops, workers tend to move from the primary sector towards the secondary and tertiary sectors.

questions.q: Distinguish between goods and services, and explain how money made exchange easier than barter.

answer.text: Goods are physical, tangible things that can be touched and stored, such as rice, cloth or a phone. Services are useful activities done for others; they are intangible and cannot be stored, such as teaching, a bus ride or a haircut. Both satisfy human wants.

In early times exchange was by barter — goods swapped directly for other goods. This was difficult because it needed a double coincidence of wants: each person had to want exactly what the other offered.
Money solved this by acting as a common medium of exchange accepted by everyone, and also as a measure and store of value, making buying and selling far easier.

questions.q: Who are producers and consumers, and how does exchange connect them?

answer.text: Producers are those who make goods or provide services. A farmer producing wheat, a factory making cloth and a doctor giving treatment are all producers, because they create something that others need.
Consumers are those who use or buy these goods and services to satisfy their needs and wants. Every one of us is a consumer when we eat food, wear clothes or use a bus.

Producers and consumers are linked through exchange. Producers sell what they make, and consumers buy what they need, usually using money. This buying and selling in markets connects those who produce with those who consume.

answer: Thus producers make goods and services, consumers use them, and exchange in the market is the link that ties the two together.

questions.q: Why are all three sectors of the economy important and dependent on one another?
answer: The economy has three sectors, primary, secondary and tertiary, and each is important and linked to the others.

answer.text: The primary sector produces goods directly from nature, such as farming, fishing and mining. The secondary sector turns these raw materials into finished goods through manufacturing, as when cotton becomes cloth. The tertiary sector provides services such as transport, trade, banking and teaching.

The sectors depend on one another. Factories in the secondary sector need raw materials from the primary sector, and both need the tertiary sector to transport, sell and finance their goods. In turn, farmers and factories buy services and finished products.
Because they are so linked, a problem in one sector affects the others.

answer: Thus all three sectors are important, and their close dependence keeps the whole economy running.
